questions.question: An EHR lists a medication as active, but the patient says it was stopped after hospitalization. What is the best FNP response?
choices: Assume the EHR is correct
Reconcile the medication using the patient account, discharge information, pharmacy or outside records as appropriate, and document the intended current plan
Delete every historical medication without review
Ignore the discrepancy if the visit is unrelated
questions.explanation: The EHR is a representation of care and may be stale or conflicting. High-risk information requires source and timeline verification followed by closed-loop reconciliation.

questions.question: Which set correctly states the clinical decision support Five Rights?
choices: Right diagnosis, drug, dose, price, and insurer
Right screen, password, server, vendor, and contract
Right information, people, intervention format, channel, and point in workflow
Right code, claim, note length, template, and billing level
questions.explanation: Effective CDS delivers the right information to the right people in the right format through the right channel at the right workflow time.

questions.question: A renal dosing alert uses a creatinine from eight months ago. What should the FNP do first?
choices: Verify the data source and freshness, assess current renal function and clinical context, and make an independent dosing decision
Accept the alert because computerized recommendations are objective
Override it without documenting or reporting the data issue
Stop all medications permanently
questions.explanation: A correct algorithm can still produce an unsafe recommendation from stale input. The clinician must verify inputs, make the patient-specific decision, and report system risk when appropriate.

questions.question: Which action best addresses alert fatigue?
choices: Make every alert interruptive
Require users to read longer warning text
Add a second alert whenever the first is overridden
Review firing, usefulness, timing, specificity, overrides, outcomes, and burden, then redesign or retire low-value alerts
questions.explanation: Alert fatigue is a systems-design problem. Targeting, workflow fit, actionability, and monitoring should determine whether an alert is improved, changed to passive support, or removed.

questions.question: What is the safest use of generative AI for clinical documentation?
choices: Automatically sign all generated notes
Use an approved tool and have the responsible clinician verify the full output against the encounter before signing
Permit the model to invent missing examination findings
Enter PHI into any free consumer chatbot if the answer is fast
questions.explanation: Approved use does not remove clinician accountability. Generated text must be verified, corrected, and limited to what actually occurred; privacy requirements still apply.

questions.question: A remote-monitoring program improves average outcomes but performs worse for patients without broadband or English proficiency. What is the best next step?
choices: Report only the overall average
Exclude those patients from evaluation
Co-design accessible alternatives, interpreter-supported workflows, and non-digital options while measuring subgroup outcomes and burden
Require portal enrollment as a condition of care
questions.explanation: Digital equity requires measuring who can access and benefit from the tool and providing clinically safe alternatives rather than widening existing barriers.

questions.question: Which statement about FDA regulation of clinical software is most accurate?
choices: Regulatory status can depend on intended use, user, output, urgency, and whether the basis can be independently reviewed; current guidance and governance should be consulted
All software used in healthcare is automatically an FDA-approved device
No AI-enabled software can be a medical device
A vendor's marketing statement determines regulatory status
questions.explanation: Digital-health oversight is use-specific. Clinicians and organizations should rely on current FDA guidance, labeling, and regulatory expertise rather than broad assumptions.

questions.question: What is the best description of interoperability?
choices: It guarantees that all exchanged data are correct
It eliminates the need for medication reconciliation
It means the receiving clinician has no responsibility for imported data
It supports exchange and use of information, but identity, source, units, definitions, completeness, and clinical meaning still require validation
questions.explanation: Technical exchange does not guarantee semantic or clinical accuracy. Imported information must still be checked for identity, provenance, completeness, and meaning.

questions.question: Which plan is essential when a clinic depends on an EHR and electronic prescribing?
choices: Assume the vendor will prevent all downtime
Maintain an approved downtime and recovery plan for identification, critical data, orders, documentation, communication, and later reconciliation
Use personal email accounts whenever the EHR is unavailable
Delay all urgent treatment until restoration
questions.explanation: Business continuity is a patient-safety function. Temporary workflows must support urgent care and be reconciled after restoration to prevent omissions and duplicates.

questions.question: What is the best way to evaluate a newly deployed AI-supported clinical tool?
choices: Measure clinician satisfaction only during the first week
Assume premarket validation applies forever
Monitor patient outcomes, false positives and negatives, workflow burden, subgroup performance, incidents, updates, and drift over time
Evaluate only how quickly the model produces an answer
questions.explanation: Real-world performance can change with populations, data, workflows, evidence, and software updates. Continuous clinical, operational, safety, and equity monitoring is required.
